column1: What is the central invariant explaining why color is NOT a property of light itself?
column2: Color is a constructed perceptual experience arising from the collision of three independent systems: electromagnetic radiation, eye physiology, and neural processing—so identical physical spectra can look different, and different spectra can look identical.

column1: What wavelength range defines human-visible light, and why is this range not a universal constant?
column2: Approximately 380 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red); it only reflects the evolutionary accident that Earth's solar output peaks there and human cones happen to be sensitive to it (e.g., mantis shrimp see 12 channels, dogs see mainly blue/yellow).

column1: Name the three human cone cell types, their approximate peak sensitivities, and the key property they share.
column2: S (~420nm, blue), M (~530nm, green), L (~560nm, red). Each responds to a broad range of wavelengths with overlapping sensitivity curves, not just its peak wavelength.

column1: What is metamerism, and why does it matter for screens?
column2: Metamerism is when two physically different spectral compositions produce identical perceived color due to cone overlap. It's why a monitor can simulate a sunset without emitting any light above 660nm or below 420nm.

column1: Why is a numerical RGB triplet like (128, 64, 200) considered 'meaningless in isolation'?
column2: Because RGB is device-dependent—the same values produce different perceived colors depending on the display's phosphor primaries, gamma curve, and white point calibration.

column1: What is color constancy, and what mechanism produces it?
column2: Color constancy is the visual system's ability to perceive an object's color as stable under varying illumination (e.g., a banana looks yellow in sun or tungsten light). It results from cones reporting relative/contrastive signals against neighboring stimuli, not absolute wavelengths.

column1: What three orthogonal perceptual attributes does HSL decouple, and what does RGB fail to separate?
column2: HSL separates hue (color family), saturation (purity/intensity), and lightness (perceived brightness). RGB bundles all three attributes inextricably together in its channel values.

column1: What are the three opponent-process channels in human color vision, and why do complementary colors create visual tension?
column2: Red-green, blue-yellow, and light-dark. Complementary colors (180° apart on the wheel) stimulate both poles of an opponent channel simultaneously, producing maximum chromatic contrast and an optical 'vibration' effect—a neurological, not cultural, response.

column1: In the 12-step color wheel, what hue-angle relationships define complementary, analogous, and triadic harmonies?
column2: Complementary: 180° apart. Analogous: adjacent hues spanning 30°–60°. Triadic: three hues at 120° intervals forming an equilateral triangle.

column1: Why can two colors with the identical hue angle (e.g., 220°) function completely differently in a composition?
column2: Because saturation and lightness independently modulate visual weight, spatial position, and emotional temperature—hue alone never fully defines a color's compositional behavior.

column1: Why can an RGB value that looks vibrant on an LED display print as a muddy orange-brown on uncoated paper?
column2: Because display color uses additive light emission while print uses subtractive light absorption—categorically different physics—so the same coordinate maps to different perceptual colors without a color management translation layer.

column1: What did Josef Albers's Interaction of Color studies demonstrate, and what practical rule follows from it?
column2: Identical color patches appear visibly different depending on their surrounding context (simultaneous contrast). Practical rule: critically evaluate color in isolation from distracting surrounding colors, e.g. using a neutral grey viewing card.
